title: SAT Test Day: Bluebook, Desmos & Pacing
summary: The digital tools and pacing that quietly win points on test day — the app, the calculator, the flag and the clock.

nodes.label: Pacing
nodes.note: ~71s per RW Q · ~95s per Math Q

chunks.heading: Know Bluebook cold
chunks.body: The SAT runs in the **Bluebook app** on your own or a provided device. It has an **on-screen countdown timer, a mark-for-review flag, an answer-eliminator, and annotation**. Master these in practice so you're **spending brain-power on questions, not the interface**.
chunks.realExample: The answer-eliminator lets you cross out wrong options with a click — using it turns a hard 4-option question into an easier 2-option guess. Small tool, real points.
chunks.memoryHook: Rehearse Bluebook's timer, flag, eliminator and annotate. Tools = free points.

chunks.heading: Use Desmos deliberately
chunks.body: The **built-in Desmos calculator works on all Math questions**. It shines for **graphing, systems of equations, and checking answers** — but for simple arithmetic or setups, reasoning is faster. Decide per question whether Desmos saves time.
chunks.realExample: Graph a quadratic to read its vertex or roots instantly; but don't fire up Desmos to compute 15% of 80 — that's slower than doing it in your head.
chunks.memoryHook: Desmos for graphs and systems; your head for quick arithmetic.

chunks.heading: Pace to finish every module
chunks.body: Budget roughly **71 seconds per Reading & Writing question** and **95 seconds per Math question**. Do a **first pass answering the ones you're sure of**, flagging the rest, then return. Finishing each module — with a guess on every question — beats perfecting a few and leaving others blank.
chunks.realExample: On RW, don't sink two minutes into one tricky logic question — flag it, keep the easy points flowing, and revisit with your leftover time.
chunks.memoryHook: ~71s RW, ~95s Math. First pass = sure ones; flag the rest; no blanks.

chunks.heading: No penalty — and superscoring helps
chunks.body: There's **no penalty for wrong answers**, so **answer every question**. Many colleges also **superscore** — taking your best section scores across test dates — so a retake to lift just one section can raise your effective total.
chunks.realExample: If your first SAT is RW 700 / Math 640, a retake that lifts Math to 720 can give a superscore of RW 700 + Math 720 — check whether your target colleges superscore.
chunks.memoryHook: Never blank (no penalty). Superscoring means a targeted retake can lift your total.

recall.q: What app is the Digital SAT taken in, and what tools does it include?
recall.a: The Bluebook app, which includes an on-screen timer, a mark-for-review flag, an answer-eliminator and annotation.

recall.q: When is the built-in Desmos calculator most useful?
recall.a: For graphing, solving systems of equations and checking answers — but quick arithmetic is often faster by reasoning.

recall.q: What's a good per-question pace for each section?
recall.a: About 71 seconds per Reading & Writing question and 95 seconds per Math question.

recall.q: Why should you answer every SAT question?
recall.a: There's no penalty for wrong answers, so a guess can only help.

recall.q: What is superscoring and why does it matter?
recall.a: Many colleges take your best section scores across test dates, so a retake that lifts one section can raise your effective total.
